name: Aaron Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 4 at Millbrook Primary, an old brick school at the bottom of Station Road in a town that used to make cloth. I'm in by half seven, photocopying because the copier jams after nine, then it's thirty-one nine-year-olds until three, and marking at the kitchen table until about eight. The best bit is when a kid who couldn't read in September reads the register out loud. The worst bit is the paperwork, the data drops every six weeks that nobody seems to read.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the pay's on the low side. How does money work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Dana, she's a care worker doing twelve-hour shifts, and between us we just about cover the rent on a two-bed flat above a bakery. I'm on the lower end of the pay scale because I moved schools and lost a point. We've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank at the end of the month. If the car fails its test, that's it, we're on the credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the staffroom: told you so. Every year someone from the trust comes in with a new app that's going to fix reading, and every year it's me and a box of phonics cards. I'd probably post something smug in the union group chat, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays as tight as it is now, and that's not nothing. Nothing changing means the pay still doesn't stretch, my girlfriend Dana's still knackered and we still can't save for a deposit. AI being hype doesn't fix the fact that teachers round here are skint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, basically. I'd stay at Millbrook, keep my head down and keep going to the union branch meetings about the pay offer. I'd try to pick up the after-school football club, which pays forty pounds a week extra, and we'd keep cutting back on takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly, that nobody's going to try to replace the bit of the job I love. But it's a tired relief. The same worries are still sitting there on the kitchen table next to the marking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned routine tasks getting automated. Is there anything in your day you'd actually hand over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The data drops, if a machine could fill those in without me learning another system, fine. But every time they've automated something at our school, it's come with a login and a training session after school. I've got six passwords already and I write them on the back of my planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dana the night you heard AI had fizzled out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her, my job's safe, love, but I'm still not earning enough to get us out of this flat. Probably we'd have a laugh about it and then do the shopping list. The flat above a bakery smells lovely but the boiler's been broken since October.

say: I'd tell the staffroom **I told you so** about all the shiny apps the trust keeps buying.
I'd post something **smug** in the union group chat about reading still needing a real teacher.
think: Nothing changing means my **pay** still doesn't stretch and we still can't save a deposit.
AI fizzling out doesn't fix the fact that **teachers round here** are skint.
do: Keep teaching Year 4 at Millbrook and keep attending **union branch meetings** about pay.
Take on the **after-school football club** for an extra forty pounds a week.
Cut back on **takeaways** to stop the credit card creeping up.
feel: Tired **relief** that nobody is coming for the part of teaching he loves.
Still **worried** about money, which sits on the kitchen table next to the marking.
S0.quote: Nothing changing means the pay still doesn't stretch, my girlfriend Dana's still knackered and we still can't save for a deposit.
fieldNote: Aaron's **money pressure** exists with or without AI, so the plateau brings no real comfort.
He treats every new school system as a **login** and a training session, not a help.
His pride sits in **reading progress** with children, the part he thinks no app touches.

steps.text: Keep teaching Year 4 at Millbrook Primary as normal
Run the after-school football club for forty pounds a week
Stop weekly takeaways to keep the credit card down
Attend union branch meetings on the pay offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say we need the union at the table before any of this goes into classrooms. Teachers aren't against change, we're against change being done to us by people who've never taught a wet Friday afternoon. I'd share every article about kids being let down by software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared. The bits of my job a computer could do are exactly the bits the trust counts, and there's only two primaries in walking distance of our flat. Marking, planning, reports, the data drops: if that's all software, someone in head office will say one teacher can have thirty-eight kids instead of thirty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a written agreement on class sizes. I'd probably have to finally learn whatever system they bring in, which I'd hate, but I'd do the bare minimum training to keep my job. And I'd stop the car, sell it, and get the bus, because we can't carry a car loan if my hours or pay get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the first week of a new Ofsted framework, when nobody knows what the rules are yet. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the bare minimum training. If the school made it compulsory, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sit at the back and do it, the same way I did the safeguarding module, and grumble. I'm not going to lose my job over being stubborn about a login. But I won't use it at home on a Sunday, that's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Millbrook would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okafor, the teaching assistant in my class. She does the reading groups, the photocopying and the spelling tests, and that's exactly what they'd say a program can do. She's got two kids and she's the reason half my class can read, and nobody in head office would ever know that.

say: I'd say the **union** has to be at the table before AI goes into classrooms.
I'd share stories about **kids being let down** by school software.
think: The tasks AI could take, like **marking and reports**, are exactly what the trust counts.
Head office could push classes to **thirty-eight kids**, and only two schools are within walking distance.
do: Push the union branch for a **written agreement** on class sizes.
Do the **minimum training** on any new system to keep his job.
Sell the **car** and take the bus to avoid a loan.
feel: **Sick** with the uncertainty, like the first week of a new inspection framework.
**Awake at night** doing sums about rent and pay.
S1.quote: The bits of my job a computer could do are exactly the bits the trust counts, and there's only two primaries in walking distance of our flat.
fieldNote: Aaron sees AI mainly as a **budget excuse** for bigger classes, not a tool.
He'll accept **compulsory training** but draws a hard line at weekend use.
His deepest concern is for **Mrs Okafor**, the teaching assistant whose tasks look most automatable.
Selling the car shows how **thin his cushion** is: he cuts transport before anything else.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a written class-size agreement
Complete the school's compulsory AI training module and nothing more
Sell the car and take the bus to school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political choice, not the weather. Governments decide whether a nine-year-old gets a person or a screen. I'd be at every march, and I'd be shouting about it online, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the thinking side of teaching could be gone by 2028: the planning, the marking, even the explaining. What's left is the hands-on part, keeping thirty kids safe, wiping noses, breaking up fights, and that's not what they pay a qualified teacher for. I think they'd keep a few of us as supervisors on lower pay, and with two weeks of money in the bank, I can't ride that out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the strike committee straight away, not just turn up. I'd start applying for teaching assistant and youth work jobs as a backup, even though it's a pay cut. Dana and I would probably have to give up the flat and move in with her mum in the next town, which nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly frightened, like when you lose a child on a school trip for five minutes. Except it wouldn't be five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots three years after the AI, does that gap change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It means for three years the job is basically crowd control, which is a person's job, so maybe I'm paid less but I'm still in the building. Then in 2031 even that goes. So I'd use those three years to fight, and to find something Dana and I can live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your pay dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, the phone contracts, the gym I never go to. Then we stop putting anything towards the wedding fund, which is about three hundred quid and a jar. I'd hate telling Dana that.

say: I'd say whether a child gets a **person or a screen** is a political choice.
I'd march and post online about it, which he **never** normally does.
think: The **thinking side** of teaching could be gone by 2028, leaving supervision on lower pay.
With **two weeks of savings**, he can't ride out a pay cut.
do: Join the **strike committee** straight away rather than just turning up.
Apply for **teaching assistant** and youth work jobs as backup.
Give up the flat and **move in** with his girlfriend's mum.
feel: Properly **frightened**, like losing a child on a school trip.
S2.quote: Governments decide whether a nine-year-old gets a person or a screen.
fieldNote: Aaron expects to keep a **supervisor role** on lower pay, then lose it when robots arrive.
He reads the three-year robot gap as **time to fight**, not to adapt.
The **wedding jar** is his most painful cut, and he dreads telling his girlfriend.

steps.text: Join the union strike committee in the first month
Apply for teaching assistant and youth work jobs nearby
Move into Dana's mum's house to save the rent
Stop paying into the wedding fund jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the fast one, that this is a choice and we've got five years to make the right one. I'd say it louder, because five years is enough time to win something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I'm thirty-two when the thinking part goes, and thirty-five when the robots come. I'd have a few years to see it, but I don't know what I'd train for, because whatever I pick, the AI gets there first. I'm not the type to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year pushing hard in the union for a guarantee: a qualified teacher in every class, written into law. I'd try to put fifty pounds a month away, even if it's just from the football club money. And I'd look at whether a special needs qualification makes me harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicky than the 2028 one, but heavy. Like knowing a storm's coming on a trip day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the type to jump. What would it take for you to jump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone like me do it and land on their feet. If a teacher I knew went into, I don't know, play therapy, and was still paying their rent a year later, I'd think about it. Until then I'd rather fight for the job I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Dana change any plans with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids in a couple of years. Honestly I'd want to wait until we knew whether I've got a job in 2031. My girlfriend Dana does care work, which is hands-on, so she might be the safe one, which is a funny thought.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough time to win a real guarantee for children.
I'd argue louder because a fight with time is a **fight you can win**.
think: He'd be **thirty-two** when thinking work goes and thirty-five when robots come.
He doesn't know what to **retrain** for, since AI gets everywhere first.
do: Campaign for a **qualified teacher** in every class written into law.
Put **fifty pounds a month** aside from the football club money.
Look into a **special needs** qualification to be harder to replace.
feel: **Heavy** but less panicky than the two-year version.
S3.quote: My girlfriend Dana does care work, which is hands-on, so she might be the safe one, which is a funny thought.
fieldNote: Aaron would only **retrain** after seeing a teacher like him land safely.
He'd **delay children** until he knows whether he has a job in 2031.
He notices his girlfriend's **hands-on care work** may outlast his teaching, which unsettles his idea of security.

steps.text: Campaign with the union for a teacher-in-every-class law
Save fifty pounds a month from football club pay
Ask about a special needs teaching qualification
Put off having children until his job looks safe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to protect children and teachers properly. I'd want the union to be writing the rules now, not reacting in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels survivable. I'd be thirty-seven, and I think by then teaching would be smaller, but there might still be a place for people who are good with the kids nobody else can reach. My worry is the pay, because a smaller profession with less bargaining power means my pay gets worse, not better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the special needs qualification over two or three years, part-time, because those kids need people, not screens. I'd try to get a full pay point back by moving up the scale. And I'd stay active in the union so there's someone at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's like an inspection that's a year away instead of next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI tools. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, slowly. If it was proven and other teachers I trust were using it to give them their evenings back, I might try it around 2030. I'm not going to be the first, I'll be the last but one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money over that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money's the thing that doesn't change. Even with ten years, I'm still starting with two weeks in the bank. The qualification costs, so I'd be asking the school to pay for it, and if they won't, I'm stuck.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift to protect children and teachers properly.
I'd want the **union writing the rules** now, not reacting later.
think: A **smaller profession** with less bargaining power would mean worse pay.
He hopes there's still a place for teachers who reach **the hardest kids**.
do: Study a **special needs** qualification part-time over two or three years.
Work to win back a **pay point** on the scale.
Stay active in the **union** so teachers have a voice.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to breathe, like an inspection a year away.
S4.quote: Even with ten years, I'm still starting with two weeks in the bank.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Aaron **plan a move** into special needs teaching, which he sees as people work.
He'd try AI around 2030 as **the last but one**, never the first.
His **savings gap** caps every plan: the qualification depends on the school paying.

steps.text: Ask the school to fund a part-time special needs qualification
Stay on the union branch committee to shape AI rules
Try AI marking tools once trusted colleagues use them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years and two weeks of savings doesn't add up to anything. What would help is a law that says every class has a qualified teacher, and some kind of pay guarantee while people retrain, so it isn't on me and Dana alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. Everyone talks about teachers' jobs, but my class has got kids whose only safe adult all day is at school. If you swap a child's only safe adult for a screen, that's not a saving, that's a cost someone else pays later.

headlineQuote: If you swap a child's only safe adult for a screen, that's not a saving, that's a cost someone else pays later.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** Year 4 teacher in a former mill town, living with his care-worker girlfriend.
He has about **two weeks of savings**, lower pay and only two primary schools in reach.
He never uses AI and sees it mainly as a **budget excuse** for bigger classes.
His answer to every scenario is the **union**, plus cutting costs and holding on.
Only with ten years does he plan a move into **special needs** teaching.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years and two weeks of savings leave no room to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: A law guaranteeing a **qualified teacher** in every class.
A **pay guarantee** while people retrain, so households aren't alone.
